name: SWE-Gym
description: The first environment for training software engineering agents, containing 2,438 real-world Python task instances, each comprising a codebase with an executable runtime environment, unit tests, and a task specified in natural language. The paper also describes SWE-Gym Lite with 230 instances and SWE-Gym Raw with 64,689 Python GitHub issues without executable environments.
creator: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang
citeAs: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang. Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym. Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025.
rai:dataCollection: SWE-Gym was constructed from real-world software engineering tasks sourced from pull requests and GitHub issues in Python repositories. The authors first used SEART GitHub search to filter repositories created before July 1, 2022 with more than 500 stars, at least 300 lines of code, more than 500 pull requests, and 100 contributors, resulting in 358 repositories. They then used SWE-Bench's instance extraction script to convert repositories into task instances containing the issue description, repository snapshot, and unit tests, yielding 64,689 raw instances. They focused on 11 repositories with numerous instances and semi-manually created executable environments for them. Dependencies were manually configured for each task instance using configuration files, CI scripts, or repository documentation, and instances were validated using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure the gold patch passed more unit tests than the original code. After validation and filtering, 2,438 unit-test-validated instances remained.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator, Document analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consisted of Python GitHub repositories, GitHub issues, pull requests, repository snapshots, unit tests, and human-submitted gold patches. SWE-Gym Raw contains 64,689 Python GitHub issues without executable environments spanning 358 Python repositories.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Repositories were selected from those created before July 1, 2022.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors associated instances with version numbers, generalized SWE-Bench's versioning script to support versioning via script execution, and semi-automatically collected versions for each instance based on repository information such as pyproject.toml and git tags. They filtered out failed instances after validation and also created a SWE-Gym Lite subset by following the SWE-Bench Lite filtering pipeline, excluding tasks requiring editing more than one file, poorly described problem statements, excessively complex ground-truth diffs, and tests focused on error message validation.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Preprocessing included filtering repositories with SEART GitHub search; extracting task instances with SWE-Bench's instance extraction script; associating instances with version numbers; setting up executable environments version-by-version; manually configuring dependencies using requirements files, CI scripts, or documentation; validating instances with SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure gold patches improved unit test results; filtering out failed instances; and releasing pre-built Docker images for reproducibility. For SWE-Gym Lite, the authors followed the SWE-Bench Lite filtering pipeline to exclude multi-file edits, poorly described tasks, overly complex diffs, and tests focused on error message validation.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human effort was used to semi-manually create executable environments and manually configure dependencies for each task instance using relevant configuration files, CI scripts, or repository documentation. The authors then used execution-based validation to verify that the human-submitted gold patch passed more unit tests than the original code. The paper states that annotations were done by a subset of the authors and that this process required approximately 200 human annotation hours.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Instances were validated using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script, and failed instances were filtered out. The paper also discusses easy-data bias in sampled successful trajectories for training, noting that repeated sampling biases toward easier tasks and proposing per-instance capping to mitigate this bias.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotations were done by a subset of the authors.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SWE-Bench's instance extraction script; SWE-Bench's versioning script; SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors state that they publicly release SWE-Gym, models, agent trajectories, pre-built Docker images for each instance, and open source all artifacts of the project including dataset, model weights, agent trajectory data, and the training pipeline. No updating timeframe or deprecation policy is specified.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that improving automated software engineering capabilities could increase developer productivity and accessibility across industries, support critical open-source infrastructure, and make software development more accessible. It also notes potential impacts on software engineering jobs and the need for careful consideration around code ownership, licensing, and attribution. The authors warn that similar techniques could potentially be misused to automate the creation of malicious code and encourage future work on responsible deployment, including security, safety, and economic impacts.
rai:dataBiases: The paper notes several biases and distribution issues. Ignoring executable environments could introduce distribution bias, diminishing SWE-Gym's utility, which motivated manual environment configuration. Task distribution across repositories exhibits a long-tail pattern, with pandas comprising nearly one-third of the total and bokeh about one percent. The authors also discuss easy-data bias in repeated sampling for training trajectories, where broader task coverage introduces a bias toward easier tasks; they mitigate this with per-instance capping. In concurrent work comparison, they state their manual configuration avoids potential dataset bias through manual configuration of environments.
rai:dataLimitations: The paper states that SWE-Gym is limited by environment diversity, including the number of repositories, types of tasks, and programming languages. It also notes that SWE-Gym currently contains tasks from 11 Python repositories and that tasks may be harder than SWE-Bench due to inclusion of sophisticated repositories like pandas and MONAI. The authors report that self-improvement results are modest and that verifier performance is imperfect, leaving a gap between Pass@k and Best@k. They also note that current SWE settings focus solely on task completion and neglect human-in-the-loop collaboration.
rai:dataUseCases: SWE-Gym is intended as a training environment for software engineering agents and verifiers. The paper uses it for rejection sampling fine-tuning of language model agents, self-improvement experiments, verifier training, inference-time scaling through reranking sampled trajectories, and research on automatic dataset synthesis and agent development. SWE-Gym Lite is described as suitable for rapid prototyping. SWE-Gym Raw is released to support future research in SWE agent development and automatic dataset synthesis.
